documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT

43 y/o woman, office administrator, transferring care from her prior primary care office (records release signed today). Main reasons for switching: access, and wanting someone who knows what HAE is.

HTN: on hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg every morning for about four years, started by the prior PCP. Home cuff readings mostly 120s/high 70s. No side effects she notices. No headaches, chest pain, swelling.

Hereditary angioedema: her mother has confirmed C1 inhibitor deficiency and the patient was told she has the same thing. Swelling episodes since she was a small child: lips, hands or feet, occasionally genital swelling, and bouts of bad crampy belly pain. Each one runs 2-3 days and goes away by itself. Antihistamines were tried years ago and did nothing. Has never been given anything specific for it and does not carry any rescue medicine. No throat involvement she can remember. Last bad episode was over a year ago.

PMH: as above. No surgeries.
Meds: HCTZ 25 mg daily.
Allergies: none to drugs, none to foods.
FH: mother HAE (C1-INH deficiency). Father with high blood pressure, had a stroke at 60.
SH: never smoker. A drink or two a month. Works full time in an office.

ROS otherwise negative.

EXAM
Vitals per flowsheet. Comfortable, well appearing.
HEENT: no lip or tongue swelling, oropharynx clear. Neck supple, no thyroid enlargement.
CV: RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear bilaterally.
Abd: soft, nontender, no masses.
Ext: no edema, no swelling of hands or feet.
Skin: no rash or urticaria.
Pelvic: normal external genitalia, cervix without lesions; Pap/HPV collected.
Neuro: grossly nonfocal.

ASSESSMENT / PLAN
1. Essential hypertension, controlled on HCTZ 25. Continue. CMP today.
2. Hereditary angioedema, C1-INH deficiency by family history and her report. Not on any HAE therapy. She is not interested in a specialist right now since attacks are infrequent. Reminded her that ACE inhibitors and estrogen-containing products should be avoided. Will revisit.
3. Health maintenance: Pap with HPV collected. Screening mammogram ordered. CBC, lipids, TSH, A1c. Offered one-time HIV and hep C screening, she agreed. Colon screening starts at 45.
4. Prior records requested.

Return after labs/records, BP check in about six months.

orders.reason: Neck pain with left arm weakness and numbness
Left arm radicular symptoms with weakness

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Two weeks of neck pain shooting into the L arm. Sharp, burning, worse when she turns her head or looks down at her laptop. Numb L thumb and index finger. No injury she can think of. No bowel/bladder change, no leg symptoms, no fever. Ibuprofen at home took the edge off a little. Pain 6/10.

O: BP as charted. Neck: tender L paraspinal muscles, rotation to the L reproduces arm pain. L elbow flexion weak compared with R; rest of arm strength full. L brachioradialis reflex reduced compared with R; biceps and triceps reflexes symmetric. Light touch reduced over L thumb and index. Gait normal.

A/P: L arm radicular pain with objective weakness and reflex change, likely C6/C7 root. Given the weakness, MRI C-spine now rather than waiting, and neurology referral. Heat, gentle range of motion, avoid heavy lifting. Call with any spreading weakness or trouble with walking or bladder.

conditions.label: Cervical degenerative disc disease with C6-C7 herniation

reports.text:
Technique: multiplanar multisequence MRI of the cervical spine without contrast.

Alignment normal. Vertebral body heights preserved; marrow signal normal. Cord normal in caliber and signal. Craniocervical junction unremarkable.

C2-C3 through C5-C6: no significant disc bulge, canal or foraminal narrowing.
C6-C7: degenerative disc desiccation with a left-sided disc herniation. Central canal patent.
C7-T1: unremarkable.
Paraspinal soft tissues normal.
reports.conclusion: C6-C7 degenerative disc disease with left-sided disc herniation at C6-C7. No cord compression.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body: C6-7 disc herniation on the left, which fits her arm symptoms. No cord compression. Called her and went over it. Neurology appointment 4/26, keep it. Sooner if weakness worsens.

documents.title: Neurology Consultation
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
OUTPATIENT NEUROLOGY CONSULTATION
Date of visit: 04/26/2021
Referring: primary care

Reason: neck pain into the left arm.

History: 46-year-old office administrator with hypertension and hereditary angioedema (C1 inhibitor deficiency). For about six weeks she has had neck pain that travels into the left arm, described as sharp and burning and aggravated by moving her neck. She notes numbness of the left thumb and index finger. No bladder or bowel symptoms, no gait trouble.

Medications: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily.
Allergies: no known drug or food allergies.
Family: mother with C1 inhibitor deficiency angioedema; father with hypertension and a stroke at age 60.
Social: never smoker, about 1-2 alcoholic drinks monthly, office work.

Examination: Alert, fluent, oriented. Cranial nerves II-XII intact. Motor: left biceps weak; remaining upper and lower limb strength full. Reflexes: left brachioradialis diminished; others 2+ and symmetric; toes downgoing. Sensation: reduced light touch over the left thumb and index finger. Spurling-type maneuver not performed. Gait and coordination normal.

Imaging: MRI cervical spine 04/08/2021 personally reviewed, C6-C7 disc herniation.

Impression: Left cervical radiculopathy due to C6-C7 intervertebral disc herniation, on a background of cervical degenerative disc disease. No myelopathic signs.

Recommendations:
1. Physical therapy for cervical radiculopathy, home exercise program.
2. Ergonomic adjustments at work; avoid prolonged neck flexion and overhead lifting.
3. If the arm weakness progresses or pain is not improving after 8-10 weeks of therapy, spine surgery opinion.
4. Follow-up with neurology as needed.

Thank you for this referral.
Outpatient Neurology

documents.title: Operative Report
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
OPERATIVE REPORT (received 06/01/2021)
Date of surgery: 05/26/2021
Procedure: elective open cholecystectomy
Anesthesia: general endotracheal
Allergies: NKDA

The patient was placed supine. After prep and drape and time-out, a right subcostal incision was made and carried down through the abdominal wall. The gallbladder was identified and dissected from the liver bed. The cystic duct and cystic artery were identified, clipped and divided. The gallbladder was removed and sent to pathology. Hemostasis in the liver bed was confirmed. The fascia was closed in layers and the skin with staples. Estimated blood loss 50 mL. No complications. Patient to recovery in stable condition.

General Surgery

documents.title: Discharge Summary
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY (received 06/01/2021)
Admitted 05/26/2021, discharged 05/28/2021, general surgery service.

Procedure: open cholecystectomy 05/26/2021, uncomplicated.
History: hypertension, hereditary angioedema, cervical disc disease.
Day-of-surgery labs: WBC 7.0, hemoglobin 13.2, platelets 250K, creatinine 0.9, total bilirubin 0.8, ALT 22, AST 25.

Hospital course: diet advanced on post-op day 1, ambulating, pain controlled on oral analgesia. No fever. Incision dry.

Discharge medications: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily (home); acetaminophen as needed for pain.
Follow-up: general surgery clinic in about 5 days for wound check and staple removal.

GENERAL SURGERY CLINIC (received 06/02/2021)
Date of visit: 05/31/2021

POD 5 from open cholecystectomy. She describes a steady, dull ache along the incision that plain acetaminophen as needed has not touched. No fevers, no nausea or vomiting, bowels moving normally. Eating well.
PMH: HTN, hereditary angioedema, cervical DDD; recently seen for left arm radiculopathy.
Meds: HCTZ 25 mg daily. NKDA.

Vitals stable. Abdomen soft. Right subcostal incision clean and well approximated, no redness, warmth or drainage. Mildly tender along the wound. No fluctuance, no crepitus. Staples removed, steri-strips applied.

Impression: expected post-operative incisional pain, no sign of wound infection or collection.
Plan: acetaminophen 1 g scheduled three times daily rather than as needed, plus ibuprofen 600 mg every 8 hours with food for one week. No lifting over 10 lb for 4 more weeks. Return as needed.

General Surgery

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT RECORD (received 10/25/2021)
Arrival: 10/22/2021 19:40   Departure: 10/23/2021 08:30

CC: belly pain and lip swelling.

HPI: 46F with hereditary angioedema (C1 inhibitor deficiency) and prior open cholecystectomy. Four hours of deep, crampy abdominal pain that does not radiate, plus swelling around the lips. She and her mother, at the bedside, describe similar episodes going back to early childhood, sometimes with swelling of the face, hands, feet or genitals, typically lasting 2-3 days and settling without treatment. Antihistamines in the past never helped. No rash, no fever, no recent illness. No throat tightness, voice change or trouble swallowing.
Meds: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. NKDA, no food allergies.
Family: mother with C1 inhibitor deficiency; a maternal uncle died in his 20s of unexplained throat swelling.
Social: never smoker, rare alcohol, office administrator.

Exam: BP 140/90, HR 105, RR 28, afebrile. Uncomfortable. Swelling around the mouth, no hives. Tongue, uvula and voice normal. Lungs clear. Abdomen diffusely tender without rebound or guarding; bowel sounds hyperactive; no organomegaly.

Results: C4 6 mg/dL (low). CBC, metabolic panel and lipase unremarkable. CT abdomen/pelvis: small bowel wall edema and small-volume ascites, no obstruction.

ED course: airway monitored, no progression. IV fluids. Kept overnight in the ED observation area; abdominal pain gradually eased and lip swelling began to recede by morning.

Impression: hereditary angioedema attack, abdominal and perioral.
Disposition: home. Follow up with primary care this week and with allergy/immunology. Return immediately for any throat or tongue swelling, voice change or trouble breathing.

documents.title: Post-ED Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen in the ED Friday night for an abdominal HAE attack with lip swelling, kept overnight, home Saturday. Record received and reviewed: low C4, CT with bowel wall edema and a little ascites.

Today: belly sore but much better, eating, lips back to normal. No throat symptoms at any point. She was shaken by it, longest attack in years. Her mother was with her and brought up the uncle who died young of throat swelling, which the patient had not mentioned before; added to family history.

Exam: vitals as charted. No facial or oral swelling. Abdomen soft, mild diffuse tenderness, no guarding.

A/P
1. Hereditary angioedema - recent abdominal attack. She is now ready to see allergy/immunology to get a rescue medication in the house and confirm her complement testing. Referral placed. Until then: ED for any throat or tongue swelling.
2. HTN - BP fine, HCTZ.
Also asked about a COVID booster; fine to get at the pharmacy.

documents.title: Allergy and Immunology Consultation
documents.author: allergy/immunology
documents.body:
ALLERGY & IMMUNOLOGY CONSULTATION (received 12/14/2021)
Visit date: 12/07/2021
Referred by primary care for hereditary angioedema.

46-year-old woman with lifelong recurrent swelling (lips, extremities, genital) and abdominal pain episodes lasting 2-3 days, never responsive to antihistamines, never urticarial. Mother has confirmed C1 inhibitor deficiency; a maternal uncle died young of throat swelling. ED visit 10/22/2021 for an abdominal and perioral attack with C4 of 6 and CT bowel wall edema. Never had laryngeal symptoms. Attack frequency historically one to three per year.
Meds: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg. No ACE inhibitor, no estrogen. NKDA.
PSH: open cholecystectomy 05/2021.

Exam: no current swelling. Oropharynx clear. Skin without urticaria.

Labs (drawn today, resulted 12/10): C4 7 mg/dL (low); C1 inhibitor antigen 9 mg/dL (low); C1 inhibitor function 24% (low).

Assessment: hereditary angioedema type 1 (low C1-INH level and function), confirmed.

Plan:
1. Icatibant 30 mg subcutaneous at the start of any attack, may repeat once after 6 hours. Two syringes to keep at home; self-injection taught today with a trainer device.
2. Any throat, tongue or voice involvement: inject and call 911.
3. Continue to avoid ACE inhibitors and estrogen-containing medicines. HCTZ is fine.
4. Before surgery, endoscopy or major dental work: short-term prophylaxis with C1 inhibitor concentrate; contact our office in advance.
5. Attack rate does not call for long-term prophylaxis at present; revisit if attacks become more frequent.
6. Follow up yearly or sooner.

Allergy & Immunology

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Annual, 47F.

New: since roughly April she has had trouble hearing out of her R ear. Noticed first on phone calls, now switches the phone to the L ear. Getting gradually worse. Intermittent ringing on the R. No ear pain, drainage, vertigo or headaches. No noise exposure or trauma.
Otherwise: HAE one attack this year, treated. Neck fine. BP fine.

Meds: HCTZ 25 mg daily; icatibant 30 mg SC prn. NKDA.
PHQ-2: 0.

Exam: Vitals as recorded. Ears: canals clear, TMs normal both sides. Whispered voice heard on L, missed on R. Face symmetric at rest and with smile today. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Breasts without masses. Abdomen soft. No edema. Neuro: no nystagmus, gait normal.

A/P
1. R-sided progressive hearing loss with tinnitus over 5 months, normal canal/TM - asymmetric hearing loss needs audiometry and ENT. Referred to ENT, who will do the audiogram there.
2. HTN controlled.
3. HAE: icatibant on hand, PA renewal due December (allergy handles).
4. Health maintenance: FIT kit, mammogram ordered, fasting labs. Flu and bivalent COVID booster at a nurse visit in October.

Technique: MRI of the brain with dedicated thin-section imaging of the internal auditory canals, before and after IV gadolinium.

A 2.0 cm enhancing mass in the right cerebellopontine angle with extension into the right internal auditory canal. No hydrocephalus. Left internal auditory canal and cerebellopontine angle normal. reports.conclusion: 2.0 cm right cerebellopontine angle mass extending into the internal auditory canal, most consistent with vestibular schwannoma.

OTOLARYNGOLOGY CONSULT (received 10/19/2022)
Seen 10/14/2022, referred by primary care.

47-year-old woman with hereditary angioedema and cervical degenerative disc disease. Six months of slowly worsening hearing in the right ear with intermittent tinnitus; over the same period she has noticed some weakness on the right side of her face. No vertigo, no headache, no change in taste.
Meds: HCTZ, icatibant as needed. NKDA.

Exam: Ear canals and tympanic membranes normal. Right corneal reflex diminished. Mild right facial droop. Remaining cranial nerves intact. No nystagmus.

Audiogram today: right sensorineural hearing loss.
MRI brain/IACs with gadolinium (10/12/2022, obtained before today's visit): 2 cm right cerebellopontine angle mass.

Impression: right acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma), 2 cm, with hearing loss, tinnitus, reduced corneal reflex and mild facial weakness.

Plan: Discussed observation, microsurgery and stereotactic radiosurgery. With symptoms and size, treatment rather than watching is favored. Referred to the skull base team (neurotology and radiation oncology) for a joint consultation. Copy to PCP.

SKULL BASE CLINIC: NEUROTOLOGY AND RADIATION ONCOLOGY (received 11/15/2022)
Visit 11/09/2022

Diagnosis: right vestibular schwannoma, 2.0 cm on MRI 10/12/2022, with right sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, diminished right corneal reflex and mild right facial weakness.
PMH: hypertension on HCTZ; hereditary angioedema type 1 (icatibant on demand); cervical DDD with prior C6-C7 radiculopathy; open cholecystectomy 2021.

Discussion: we reviewed microsurgical resection (translabyrinthine or retrosigmoid) and single-session stereotactic radiosurgery, including tumor control rates, the risk to facial nerve function and to remaining hearing with each, recovery time, and the need for MRI surveillance after radiosurgery. Her HAE adds airway and anesthesia considerations to open surgery.

Decision: she prefers stereotactic radiosurgery. Planning MRI and frame/mask fitting to be scheduled; treatment targeted for January 2023.

RADIOSURGERY TREATMENT SUMMARY (received 01/24/2023)
Treatment date: 01/18/2023

Diagnosis: right vestibular schwannoma, 2.0 cm.
Technique: single-fraction stereotactic radiosurgery with a planning MRI fused to CT the same morning. Marginal dose 12 Gy.
Course: treatment delivered without interruption. No nausea, headache or new deficit afterward. Discharged home the same day with a companion.

Post-treatment: may notice temporary fatigue or a mild increase in tinnitus over the next weeks. Follow-up MRI at 6 months, then yearly. Call for new facial weakness, imbalance or severe headache.

Allergies: NKDA. HAE: no airway manipulation required; icatibant available.

Radiation Oncology / Neurotology

documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
ENDOCRINOLOGY NEW PATIENT CONSULTATION (received 11/01/2023)
Date of visit: 10/30/2023
Self-referred. Copy to primary care.

HPI: 48-year-old woman with hypertension, hereditary angioedema, cervical disc disease and a prior workup for cervical radiculopathy, and a right acoustic neuroma treated with radiosurgery this year. Over the last few months she has had spells of severe headache with a pounding heartbeat and drenching sweats, coming more often and more intensely lately. She denies chest pain, shortness of breath or recent illness.
Meds: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily; icatibant 30 mg SC as needed. NKDA.
Family history: notable for thyroid cancer in her father. Mother with hereditary angioedema.
Social: never smoker, rare alcohol.

Exam: BP 220/110, HR 118, afebrile. Well-nourished woman, distressed with a headache during the visit. Skin moist. Fine tremor of the outstretched hands. Abdomen unremarkable.

In clinic: glucose 110, potassium 3.8, creatinine 0.9. ECG: sinus tachycardia, no ST or T changes.

Given the severity of the BP she was moved to our monitored treatment area and given intravenous phentolamine; BP came down to 150/90 and the headache and sweating settled. Observed for 2 hours before going home with a companion.

Assessment: paroxysms of headache, palpitations and diaphoresis with severe hypertension. Pheochromocytoma suspected.

Plan:
1. Plasma free metanephrines and 24-hour urine catecholamines sent today.
2. Avoid beta-blockers until alpha blockade is established; avoid decongestants and stimulants.
3. If biochemistry is positive, adrenal-protocol CT.
4. ED precautions for severe headache, chest pain or a sustained BP over 180.
5. Results visit in 1-2 weeks.

Endocrinology

events.reason: Results: catecholamine testing and adrenal CT

reports.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
reports.text:
Adrenal protocol CT of the abdomen with unenhanced, portal venous and delayed images; pelvis included on the venous phase. Status post cholecystectomy.
Left adrenal gland: 3.4 cm heterogeneous, avidly enhancing mass, attenuation 38 HU on unenhanced images. Right adrenal gland normal. Liver, spleen, pancreas and kidneys normal. No lymphadenopathy. No ascites. Pelvic organs unremarkable.
reports.conclusion: 3.4 cm heterogeneous enhancing left adrenal mass; with elevated normetanephrine, consistent with pheochromocytoma.

Visit 11/08/2023

- Plasma free normetanephrine 1136 pg/mL (reference <148) - elevated
- Plasma free metanephrine 38 pg/mL (reference <57) - normal
- 24-hour urine norepinephrine 412 mcg (reference 15-80) - elevated; epinephrine 9 mcg - normal
- Adrenal CT 11/07/2023: 3.4 cm heterogeneous enhancing left adrenal mass, 38 HU unenhanced

Assessment: left adrenal pheochromocytoma, noradrenergic.

Plan:
1. Start doxazosin 2 mg at bedtime; increase to 4 mg on 11/20 and to 8 mg on 12/04 if tolerated, guided by home BP and orthostatic symptoms.
2. Liberal salt and fluid intake once alpha blockade starts.
3. Referred to endocrine surgery for laparoscopic left adrenalectomy, target early January.
4. Germline genetic testing to be sent at the post-operative visit, given the family history of thyroid cancer and as recommended for all pheochromocytoma.
5. Allergy/immunology to coordinate peri-operative C1 inhibitor prophylaxis.
Continue hydrochlorothiazide for now.

Endocrinology

reports.text:
Specimen: left adrenal gland, laparoscopic adrenalectomy.
Gross: adrenal gland with a 3.3 cm well-circumscribed tan-red nodule.
Microscopic: nested (zellballen) pattern of polygonal cells with granular cytoplasm, supported by sustentacular cells. Tumor confined to the adrenal gland. Margins negative. Adjacent adrenal cortex unremarkable.

documents.title: Operative Report
documents.author: endocrine surgery
documents.body:
OPERATIVE REPORT (received 01/17/2024)
Date: 01/10/2024
Procedure: laparoscopic left adrenalectomy
Preop diagnosis: left adrenal pheochromocytoma, alpha-blocked on doxazosin 8 mg.
Anesthesia: general endotracheal with arterial line. C1 inhibitor concentrate given intravenously before induction per allergy/immunology for hereditary angioedema.

Lateral decubitus positioning. Four ports. The splenic flexure and spleen were mobilized, the left adrenal vein was identified and ligated early, and the gland was dissected free and removed intact in a retrieval bag. Intraoperative BP lability was managed by anesthesia with short-acting agents. EBL minimal. No complications.

documents.title: Discharge Summary
documents.author: endocrine surgery

DISCHARGE SUMMARY (received 01/17/2024)
Admitted 01/10/2024, discharged 01/12/2024.

Procedure: laparoscopic left adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma (pathology final 01/15: pheochromocytoma 3.3 cm, confined, margins negative).
Course: one night in step-down for BP and glucose monitoring, no hypotension requiring pressors, glucose normal. No angioedema. Diet resumed POD 1.

Medication changes: doxazosin STOPPED. Continue hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. Icatibant as needed (unchanged).
Follow-up: endocrine surgery 2 weeks; endocrinology in 6-8 weeks with plasma metanephrines.

ENDOCRINOLOGY FOLLOW-UP (received 03/19/2024)
Visit 03/12/2024

Two months after laparoscopic left adrenalectomy. No spells since surgery; headaches and sweating gone. Home BP 118-128/74-82 on HCTZ alone.

Plasma free normetanephrine 96 pg/mL and metanephrine 30 pg/mL - both normal.
Germline pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma panel (RET, VHL, SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SDHAF2, NF1, MAX, TMEM127, FH): no pathogenic variants identified.

Assessment: pheochromocytoma, resected, biochemically cured; no hereditary syndrome found.
Plan: plasma metanephrines yearly; return sooner for recurrent spells. BP management back to primary care.

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT RECORD (received 04/28/2025)
Arrival 04/23/2025 15:10, discharged 21:20.

CC: racing heart and lightheadedness.

HPI: 50-year-old woman with hypertension, hereditary angioedema (C1 inhibitor deficiency), cervical degenerative disc disease and a pheochromocytoma removed last year. About 30 minutes before arrival, while gardening, she felt her heart start racing and became lightheaded. Her hypertension is well controlled on hydrochlorothiazide; no known heart disease. No chest pain, no syncope.
Meds: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily; icatibant as needed. NKDA.

Exam: BP 130/85, HR 170, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air. Lungs clear. No leg swelling.

Monitor/ECG: regular narrow-QRS tachycardia, no visible P waves.

ED course: IV access placed. Adenosine given IV: the ventricular rate slowed briefly, revealing sawtooth flutter waves, and the tachycardia then resumed. Diltiazem IV given for rate control. Spontaneous conversion to sinus rhythm at about 18:30; repeat ECG sinus rhythm 76, normal. Observed further in sinus rhythm.
Labs: CBC, BMP, magnesium and TSH normal; high-sensitivity troponin normal.

Impression: atrial flutter, converted to sinus rhythm.
Disposition: home. No new medications. Please arrange outpatient cardiology follow-up. Return for recurrent palpitations, chest pain, fainting or shortness of breath.

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT RECORD (received 10/28/2025)
Arrival 10/19/2025 13:50. Admitted to the stroke service 18:10.

CC: dizziness, vomiting, trouble walking.

HPI: 50-year-old woman with cervical degenerative disc disease and a C6-C7 herniation previously evaluated for radiculopathy. Symptoms began about two hours before arrival right after she tipped her head back to paint a ceiling: the room spinning, two episodes of vomiting, numbness of the left side of her face, and weakness of the right arm and leg.
PMH also: hypertension, hereditary angioedema, atrial flutter (ED 04/2025), pheochromocytoma resected 2024, right vestibular schwannoma after radiosurgery.
Meds: hydrochlorothiazide. NKDA.

Exam: BP 150/90, HR 85, afebrile. Light touch and pinprick reduced over the left face. Right arm and leg weaker than the left. Other cranial nerves normal.

CT head without contrast: no acute abnormality.

Impression: acute posterior circulation stroke syndrome. Stroke team consulted at the bedside. Admitted to the stroke unit for MRI and workup.

reports.text:
MRI brain without contrast with diffusion-weighted imaging, plus time-of-flight MR angiography of the head and contrast-enhanced MR angiography of the neck.
Brain: focus of restricted diffusion with corresponding FLAIR signal in the left ventral midbrain at the cerebral peduncle, consistent with acute infarct. No hemorrhage. No other acute infarct. Treated right cerebellopontine angle schwannoma, unchanged. Ventricles normal.
MRA head: normal circle of Willis, basilar and posterior cerebral arteries patent, no stenosis or occlusion.
MRA neck: carotid and vertebral arteries patent without dissection, stenosis or occlusion.
reports.conclusion: Acute left ventral midbrain (cerebral peduncle) infarct. No dissection, stenosis or large-vessel occlusion.

reports.text: Normal left ventricular size and wall thickness. LVEF 60%. Normal right ventricle. Atria normal in size. No intracardiac thrombus. Valves structurally normal without significant regurgitation. Agitated saline study: no shunt. No pericardial effusion.
reports.conclusion: Normal study. EF 60%, no thrombus, no shunt.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY - STROKE SERVICE (received 10/28/2025)
Admitted 10/19/2025, discharged 10/23/2025.

Principal diagnosis: Weber syndrome - acute left midbrain (cerebral peduncle) infarction.

Presentation: vertigo, vomiting, left facial numbness and right arm and leg weakness after neck extension while painting; head CT negative in the ED.

Neurology examination on the morning of 10/20: left ptosis, left pupil larger than right, limited adduction and elevation of the left eye (partial left third nerve palsy); right arm and leg weakness; decreased sensation of the left face as noted in the ED. Speech clear.

Workup:
- MRI brain: acute left ventral midbrain infarct. MRA head and neck: no dissection, stenosis or occlusion.
- TTE: EF 60%, no thrombus, no shunt.
- Telemetry: sinus rhythm throughout the stay.
- LDL 94 mg/dL. A1c normal.

Assessment: infarct of the left midbrain producing Weber syndrome. With no vessel disease or dissection and a documented episode of atrial flutter in April 2025, the mechanism is felt to be cardioembolic.

Treatment: apixaban 5 mg twice daily started on 10/21/2025. Statin not started: LDL 94 with a cardioembolic mechanism and no atherosclerotic disease.

Course: right-sided strength improving, walking with standby assistance by day 3 and independently on discharge; ptosis improving. Swallow screen passed.

Discharge medications:
- Apixaban 5 mg by mouth twice daily - NEW
- Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily - continue
- Icatibant 30 mg SC as needed - continue

Follow-up: outpatient physical therapy; stroke clinic in 6-8 weeks; cardiology; primary care in 1-2 weeks.
Allergies: NKDA.

Admitted 04/20/2026, discharged 04/23/2026.

Principal diagnosis: acute pancreatitis, drug-induced (hydrochlorothiazide suspected).

History: hypertension; hereditary angioedema type 1; left midbrain infarct (Weber syndrome) 10/2025 on apixaban; atrial flutter 04/2025; pheochromocytoma resected 01/2024; treated right vestibular schwannoma; cervical DDD; open cholecystectomy 2021.
Medication reconciliation (pharmacy fill history and patient): hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, icatibant as needed. The ED triage list had recorded hydrochlorothiazide only.

Course: Admission lipase 850, amylase 900. RUQ ultrasound: no gallbladder, common duct 5 mm, no stones. No alcohol excess; triglycerides 180 and calcium 9.2 do not explain it. With other causes excluded and a thiazide as her only long-term drug besides apixaban, the pancreatitis was attributed to hydrochlorothiazide. Treated with IV fluids and analgesia; pain settled and diet advanced by day 3. Lipase 140 on 04/22. No angioedema during the stay.

Discharge medications:
- Hydrochlorothiazide - STOPPED (suspected cause of pancreatitis; avoid thiazides)
- Amlodipine 5 mg by mouth daily - NEW, for blood pressure
- Apixaban 5 mg by mouth twice daily - continue
- Icatibant 30 mg SC as needed - continue

Follow-up: primary care in 1-2 weeks for BP and medication review.
Allergies/intolerances: NKDA; hydrochlorothiazide - pancreatitis (added this admission).
